t: #3670 Maximum Product of Two Integers With No Common Bits
o: Find two elements whose bitwise AND is 0 maximizing their product; values are at most 1e6 < 2^20. Brute force is O(n^2) — too slow for n = 1e5. Instead use a subset-maximum (SOS) DP: let g[mask] be the largest array value whose set bits are a subset of mask. Then for each value x, the best partner compatible with x is g[complement(x)], and the answer is max x * g[~x & FULL].
k: 'No common bits' means x & y == 0, i.e., y is a submask of ~x.
SOS (sum-over-subsets, here max-over-subsets) DP computes g[mask] = max value that is a submask of mask in O(2^B * B) with B = 20.
Since x is never a submask of ~x (x > 0), g[~x] always refers to a different element, so distinctness is automatic.

a.i: Seed g[v] = v for every occurring value v, then for each bit b propagate g[mask] = max(g[mask], g[mask without bit b]). Afterwards each x pairs with the largest submask of its complement.
s: Set FULL = 2^20 - 1; initialize g[x] = max(g[x], x) for each x in nums.
For each bit b, for each mask containing b, relax g[mask] with g[mask ^ (1<<b)].
For each x, candidate = x * g[FULL ^ x] if that g is nonzero.
a.t: O(2^B * B + n) with B = 20 — the SOS DP dominates (~2e7 operations).
a.sp: O(2^B) for the g table (~1M entries).

w: The SOS trick converts an O(n^2) pairwise compatibility search into linear scans over bitmask space. Pitfall: products up to 1e12 need 64-bit results; also confirm the distinct-index argument (x cannot be a submask of its own complement since x >= 1). Follow-up: if values reached 2^31 you would instead meet-in-the-middle over high bits or use a trie on complements.
